title: Q5–6: om, and the person of sixteen parts (5–6)
hook: the last two students ask about om and about a person made of sixteen parts, and one of them admits he once had to say, I don't know
carry: the sixteen parts return to the sea

segments.voice: Yesterday: the fourth question, who is awake in sleep. Breath keeps the house, and under it, the one who sees. Today, the Prashna ends.

Sukesha, the sixth student, opens with a story against himself. A prince of Kosala once came to me, he says, and asked: do you know the person of sixteen parts? I said, I don't know. If I knew, why wouldn't I tell you? Whoever speaks what isn't true dries up to the root, so I can't speak falsely. The prince got into his chariot without a word, and left. Now, Sukesha says to Pippalada, I'm asking you. Where is that person?
screen: `DO YOU KNOW THE SIXTEEN PARTS?` → `I DON'T KNOW.` → `A LIE DRIES UP TO THE ROOT.`

segments.voice: First, the fifth question, from Satyakama. What does a person win who meditates on om until the end of life? Pippalada says om is both the higher and the lower Brahman, and its sounds open different worlds. Meditate on one of its three sounds, and you come quickly back to the human world. On two, and you go to the world of the moon, and return. But one who meditates on all three, the whole of om, is freed from wrong the way a snake slips out of its old skin. Then Sukesha's question. Where is the person of sixteen parts? Right here, Pippalada says, inside the body. And he tells how the sixteen arise. The self thought: when I leave, who will leave with me? It made breath. From breath, faith. Then space, wind, light, water, earth, the senses, mind and food. From food, strength. Then discipline, sacred verses, action, the worlds, and finally, name. Sixteen: everything a life is made of. Then an image. As rivers flowing toward the sea reach it and disappear, their names and shapes broken up, and people simply say, the sea, so these sixteen parts reach the person and disappear. Their names are gone. People simply say, the person. And that one is without parts, and deathless. The six students honored Pippalada: you are our father, who carries us across our ignorance to the farther shore. Six questions began with a teacher saying, if we know. They end with students saying, thank you.
screen: `OM: THE HIGHER AND THE LOWER.` · `LIKE A SNAKE OUT OF ITS SKIN.` · `SIXTEEN PARTS, FROM BREATH TO NAME.` · `RIVERS REACH THE SEA AND LOSE THEIR NAMES.` · then, large: `THE PERSON WITHOUT PARTS.`

segments.voice: Begin where the list of sixteen begins: one breath in, one breath out. Then let a few of the others pass through your attention, in no hurry: faith, the space around you, the warmth of the body, the food you ate, the work of your hands, and last of all, your name. Don't hold on to any of it; come back to the breath, and stay there.
Q5 and 6, the last two questions. Om opens the higher and lower worlds; the person of sixteen parts is right here, and the parts return to it like rivers to the sea.

segments.voice: Your line: the sixteen parts return to the sea. Tomorrow, a new Upanishad splits all knowing in two. That's day four hundred ten.

howItsDone: Om is commonly chanted at the start and close of Hindu prayer and study, and some teachers use the Prashna's line about a lie drying a person up to the root when they speak about truthfulness.

chat.says: Where is this person of sixteen parts the old text talks about?
options: Right here in the body; its parts return to it like rivers to the sea.
In a prince's palace far off in Kosala, hidden from Sukesha's eyes.
Nowhere at all; the old teacher admits he doesn't know it either.
chat.meaning: Pippalada says the person of sixteen parts is right here in the body; its parts reach it like rivers reaching the sea, and lose their names.

Sukesha.meaning: the sixth student, who asks about the sixteen parts

Kosala.meaning: an ancient kingdom of northern India

Satyakama.meaning: the fifth student, who asks about om

om.meaning: the sacred syllable, chanted at the start and close of prayer

Pippalada.meaning: the sage who answers the six students' questions

notes: Prashna 5: the measures of om (one, two, three) and their worlds simplified to 'one part... two parts... the whole of om'; the text speaks of three matras and the Brahma-world. Confirm the simplification is fair.
The sixteen (6.4) given from memory: prana, shraddha, kha, vayu, jyotis, apah, prthivi, indriya, manas, annam, viryam, tapas, mantrah, karma, lokah, nama. Confirm.
Hiranyanabha of Kosala is the prince; not named in the script.
Rivers image here anticipates Mundaka 3.2.8 on day 420, which will refer back.
